newsitem.title: UK: UK house price inflation to slow this year - RICS.
newsitem.headline: UK house price inflation to slow this year - RICS.

text.p: The prospect of higher interest rates, more property coming onto the market and the possible abolition of tax relief on mortgage payments will curb British house price inflation later this year, the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors said on Tuesday.

But for now, the RICs said the net balance of chartered surveyors reporting price increases rose to 60.5 percent over the three months to April 30 compared with 58.5 percent last month and only 16.6 percent in April last year.
Stocks of property for sale were 30 percent lower than in the same period last year. It is that lack of supply that is driving prices higher in many areas, it said.

The Institution said Britain's housing recovery remained strongest in London, the South and the Midlands. It said house price inflation should certainly cool off in the capital where "unsustainable" rises of up to 20 percent per annum have been seen in some areas.

More properties should come onto the market this year and rein in house prices. And with the Bank of England given independence to set interest rates, mortgage costs could shoot higher than many expect this year, it said.

"Stock shortages should ease before the end of a year in which interest rates are more likely to rise faster and higher since the Bank of England was granted independence," said RICs housing spokesman Ian Perry.

In the longer-term, the Bank's new-found independence would be good news for the housing market, he said, as it should deliver more stable interest rates. "One likely consequence will be to reduce the cost of fixed rate mortgages bringing much-needed equilibrium to the market."
In the near-term, much also depends on Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's forthcoming budget, expected within weeks.

Economists say a significant degree of fiscal tightening is required to cool domestic demand and many are advising Brown to cut or abolish mortgage interest tax relief. But Perry said the abolition of MIRAS would destabilise the housing market.

"We could see a widening of the North/South divide as the loss of MIRAS -- which covers only the first 30,000 stg of a mortgage -- would deal a bigger blow to homeowners in the North where average prices are lower than in the South," he said.
If MIRAS has to be abolished, Perry urged the Chancellor to do it gradually to keep the housing market on an even keel.
